questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Circular 230 and practice before the IRS — regulations governing practice, types of IRS representation, preparer penalties §6694/§6695, PTIN requirements
questions.text: Under Treasury Circular 230, which individuals are generally authorized to represent taxpayers before all levels of the Internal Revenue Service, including appeals and collections?

answers.text: Attorneys, certified public accountants (CPAs), and enrolled agents — all three hold unlimited practice rights before the IRS
Any individual who prepares a tax return for compensation — paid preparers automatically have full IRS representation rights
Only enrolled agents — CPAs and attorneys must obtain a separate IRS credential to practice before the IRS
Family members and legal guardians — immediate family members can represent taxpayers without any credential

explanations.a: Treasury Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10) governs practice before the Internal Revenue Service. Three categories of professionals have UNLIMITED practice rights — they may represent clients before any office of the IRS, including audits, Appeals, Collections, and the Taxpayer Advocate Service: (1) Attorneys: admitted to practice law in any US state; (2) Certified Public Accountants (CPAs): licensed by a state board of accountancy; (3) Enrolled Agents (EAs): federally authorized tax practitioners who have either passed a comprehensive three-part IRS examination or have qualifying IRS experience. Additional categories with limited rights: enrolled actuaries, enrolled retirement plan agents, and Annual Filing Season Program completers.
explanations.b: Paid preparers who are not attorneys, CPAs, or enrolled agents have LIMITED representation rights. Under Circular 230, non-credentialed preparers who have Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP) record of completion can represent clients only before revenue agents, customer service representatives, and similar IRS personnel during examination of a return they prepared — they cannot represent clients before Appeals or Collection. Full representation rights require attorney, CPA, or enrolled agent status.
explanations.c: CPAs do not need a separate IRS credential. Their state CPA license gives them unlimited practice rights before the IRS under Circular 230. Only individuals who are NOT attorneys, CPAs, or enrolled agents need to qualify separately for practice rights.
explanations.d: Family member representation is permitted in specific, limited circumstances (e.g., a family member may appear before the IRS as a witness or to provide documents), but this does not constitute authorized 'practice before the IRS' under Circular 230 and does not grant representation rights equivalent to credentialed practitioners.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Circular 230 and practice before the IRS — regulations governing practice, types of IRS representation, preparer penalties §6694/§6695, PTIN requirements
questions.text: A CPA prepares a client's federal income tax return and takes a tax position that the CPA believes has a 25% chance of being sustained if challenged by the IRS. The CPA does not disclose this position on the return. Under §6694(a), which standard applies, and is the CPA potentially subject to a preparer penalty?

answers.text: No penalty applies — a 25% probability of success satisfies the 'realistic possibility of success' standard that applies to all tax return positions

The CPA is potentially subject to the §6694(a) penalty because a 25% probability does not meet the 'substantial authority' standard (approximately 40%+ probability) required for non-disclosed positions on non-tax-shelter items
The CPA is potentially subject to the §6694(b) penalty for willful understatement, because any position with less than 50% chance is considered willful
No penalty applies to CPAs — §6694 only applies to enrolled agents and non-credentialed preparers, not to licensed CPAs

explanations.a: The 'realistic possibility of success' was the old standard under prior law. Current §6694(a) requires that the position meet the SUBSTANTIAL AUTHORITY standard for non-disclosed positions on items other than tax shelters. Substantial authority is generally interpreted as approximately a 40%+ probability of being sustained — 25% falls short.
explanations.b: Section §6694(a) imposes a penalty on a tax return preparer for understatement of a taxpayer's liability due to an UNREASONABLE POSITION. For a non-disclosed, non-tax-shelter position, the standard is SUBSTANTIAL AUTHORITY (approximately 40%+ likelihood of success if challenged). A 25% probability does not meet the substantial authority threshold. Penalty: the GREATER of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived by the preparer from the return with the unreasonable position. Exceptions: the preparer can avoid the penalty by making adequate disclosure of the position on the return AND the position has a reasonable basis (approximately 10%+ probability). If the position were disclosed (Form 8275), the lower 'reasonable basis' standard would apply and 25% probability might satisfy it. The CPA's failure to disclose triggers the higher substantial authority requirement.
explanations.c: Section §6694(b) covers WILLFUL or RECKLESS understatements — situations where the preparer knows the position is wrong or deliberately ignores facts. A 25% probability position taken in good faith (without disclosure) is more appropriately analyzed under §6694(a) for unreasonable (not willful) positions. The penalty for §6694(b) is greater: the larger of $5,000 or 75% of income from the return.
explanations.d: Section §6694 applies to ALL tax return preparers, including CPAs, attorneys, and enrolled agents. The statute explicitly covers any person who prepares for compensation any return or claim for refund. Licensed status does not exempt a preparer from §6694 penalties.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Circular 230 and practice before the IRS — regulations governing practice, types of IRS representation, preparer penalties §6694/§6695, PTIN requirements
questions.text: A paid tax return preparer fails to: (1) sign the return before delivery to the client, (2) retain a copy of the return, and (3) provide the client with a copy of the completed return. Under §6695, what is the maximum total penalty for these failures?

answers.text: $60 total — there is one combined penalty for all administrative failures regardless of the number of violations
$6,000 total — the penalty is $2,000 per violation per return for each administrative failure
$180 total — §6695 imposes a separate $60 penalty for each distinct failure (failure to sign, failure to retain copy, failure to provide copy to taxpayer)
No penalty — administrative failures by a preparer are not subject to penalties under §6695 unless the taxpayer suffers actual monetary harm

explanations.a: Section §6695 imposes SEPARATE penalties for each distinct administrative failure — they are independent violations with individual penalty amounts, not a single combined penalty.
explanations.b: $2,000 per violation does not reflect the §6695 penalty structure. The §6695 penalties are $60 per return per type of failure (subject to inflation adjustment), not $2,000.
explanations.c: Section §6695 imposes the following separate penalties on tax return preparers for administrative failures (each $60 per return as of 2023, subject to annual inflation adjustments): (1) §6695(a): failure to furnish a copy of the return to the taxpayer — $60 penalty; (2) §6695(b): failure to sign the return — $60 penalty; (3) §6695(d): failure to retain a copy or list of returns prepared — $60 penalty; (4) §6695(c): failure to provide identifying number (PTIN) — $60 penalty; (5) §6695(e): failure to file information returns — $60 per failure. For the three violations described (failure to sign + failure to retain + failure to furnish copy): 3 × $60 = $180 maximum penalty. The maximum penalty for §6695 failures in any calendar year is generally limited to $30,000 per category, preventing catastrophic penalties for high-volume preparers who make systematic errors.
explanations.d: Section §6695 penalties are strict liability — no showing of actual harm to the taxpayer is required. These are administrative penalties designed to enforce minimum professional standards for paid tax preparers. The taxpayer does not need to suffer financial loss for the penalties to apply.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Circular 230 and practice before the IRS — regulations governing practice, types of IRS representation, preparer penalties §6694/§6695, PTIN requirements
questions.text: A Circular 230 practitioner receives a legal fee of $50,000 to represent a client in a Tax Court case. The practitioner has a contingent fee arrangement: payment is contingent on the amount of tax saved. The practitioner also receives confidential client information during the engagement. Upon conclusion of the matter, a third party requests the client's tax file. Analyze the Circular 230 compliance issues presented.

answers.text: No compliance issues exist — contingent fees are always permissible for Tax Court representation, and practitioners may share client files with third parties upon request
Circular 230 prohibits ALL contingent fee arrangements for practitioners in any tax matter; sharing the file without client consent violates confidentiality obligations

The contingent fee is permissible only if it does not exceed $50,000 and the practitioner files a disclosure statement with the IRS; confidentiality rules allow disclosure to third parties for billing purposes

Circular 230 generally prohibits contingent fee arrangements for preparing original returns and other non-contested matters, but permits contingent fees in proceedings before courts (Tax Court) and in connection with IRS examination matters where the IRS has raised an issue; the practitioner must obtain client consent before disclosing client information to third parties

explanations.a: Circular 230 does not broadly permit all contingent fees. It specifically restricts contingent fees in certain contexts (original return preparation) while permitting them in others (judicial proceedings, IRS examinations when the IRS has raised an issue). Sharing client files without consent violates §10.20 and §10.28 of Circular 230.
explanations.b: Circular 230 does not prohibit ALL contingent fees. Under §10.27, contingent fee PROHIBITIONS apply to: preparation of original returns, preparation of amended returns or claims for refund if the client has not been notified by the IRS of an examination. Contingent fees ARE permitted for: judicial proceedings (Tax Court, District Court); claims for refund filed after the client has been notified of an IRS examination; and matters where a fee is based on the results achieved.
explanations.c: There is no dollar threshold for contingent fees and no required disclosure statement to the IRS regarding fee arrangements. The permissibility of contingent fees depends on the TYPE of matter, not the dollar amount.
explanations.d: Circular 230 analysis: (1) Contingent fee in Tax Court proceeding: §10.27 permits contingent fees for 'representation before a court' and for 'refund claims filed after the IRS has notified the client of an examination.' Representation in Tax Court qualifies — the $50,000 contingent fee is PERMISSIBLE in this context; (2) Confidentiality: §10.20 and §10.28 of Circular 230 require practitioners to protect confidential client information. The client's tax information may not be shared with third parties without: (a) the client's informed consent, (b) a legal requirement or court order, or (c) to comply with applicable law. A third-party request alone does not authorize disclosure — the practitioner must obtain the client's written consent before sharing the tax file.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: IRC §6662/§6663 accuracy-related penalties and authoritative hierarchy — negligence, substantial understatement, fraud penalty; substantial authority, MLTN standards; hierarchy of authority
questions.text: In the hierarchy of federal tax authority, which source ranks HIGHEST and is therefore binding on both the IRS and taxpayers?

answers.text: The Internal Revenue Code (IRC), as enacted by Congress under its constitutional taxing authority — the IRC is the primary statutory source of federal tax law
Treasury Regulations — regulations are the IRS's official interpretation of the IRC and are the most authoritative source of tax law
Revenue Rulings — the IRS's published positions on specific factual situations represent the highest authority
IRS Publications and Instructions — these represent the IRS's official guidance to taxpayers and are binding on all parties

explanations.a: The complete hierarchy of federal tax authority (highest to lowest): (1) US Constitution — supreme law, grants Congress taxing authority; (2) Internal Revenue Code (IRC) — enacted by Congress pursuant to Constitutional authority; primary statutory source; (3) Treasury Regulations — Treasury/IRS interpretation of IRC; generally binding; (4) Revenue Rulings — IRS official positions on specific fact patterns; (5) Revenue Procedures — IRS procedural guidance; (6) Private Letter Rulings — binding only on the requesting taxpayer; (7) IRS Publications — informational only; not binding. The IRC ranks at the top of the administrative sources because it is an Act of Congress — only a court ruling or Congressional amendment can override it.
explanations.b: Treasury Regulations (26 CFR) are the Treasury Department's official interpretation of the IRC and are generally binding on both taxpayers and the IRS. They rank very high in the hierarchy. However, regulations are secondary to the IRC itself — if a regulation conflicts with the IRC, the IRC prevails. Regulations are the highest ADMINISTRATIVE authority, but they rank below the IRC as statutory law.
explanations.c: Revenue Rulings represent the IRS's official position on specific factual situations. They are binding on IRS agents and can be relied upon by taxpayers, but they rank below both the IRC and Treasury Regulations. Revenue Rulings do not have the force of law in the same sense as the IRC or regulations.
explanations.d: IRS Publications (e.g., Publication 17, Publication 505) are educational materials that summarize tax rules for taxpayers. They are explicitly NOT binding on the IRS or on courts — they can contain errors, simplifications, or outdated information. Reliance on a publication does not protect a taxpayer from penalties if the publication is incorrect.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: IRC §6662/§6663 accuracy-related penalties and authoritative hierarchy — negligence, substantial understatement, fraud penalty; substantial authority, MLTN standards; hierarchy of authority
questions.text: A taxpayer understates their federal income tax liability by $8,000 due to negligent disregard of tax rules. The taxpayer's correct tax liability was $20,000. The understatement meets the 'substantial understatement' threshold. Calculate the §6662 accuracy-related penalty and identify whether the reasonable cause exception could apply.

answers.text: Penalty = $6,000 (75% × $8,000); reasonable cause is not a defense to accuracy-related penalties
Penalty = $1,600 (20% × $8,000); reasonable cause and good faith reliance on a tax advisor could eliminate the penalty
Penalty = $1,600 (20% × $8,000); the penalty cannot be avoided because negligence is per se unreasonable
Penalty = $3,200 (40% × $8,000); the gross valuation misstatement rate applies to all substantial understatements

explanations.a: 75% is the fraud penalty rate under §6663, not the accuracy-related penalty rate. The §6662 accuracy-related penalty is 20%. Additionally, §6664(c) provides a reasonable cause and good faith exception — it is a valid defense to §6662 penalties (though not to §6663 fraud penalties).
explanations.b: Section §6662 accuracy-related penalty: 20% × $8,000 understatement = $1,600. The §6662 penalty covers multiple components — when both negligence and substantial understatement apply, the penalty is NOT stacked (only one 20% penalty applies to the full underpayment). Reasonable cause exception (§6664(c)): the §6662 penalty does not apply to any portion of an underpayment if: (1) there was reasonable cause for the underpayment; and (2) the taxpayer acted in good faith with respect to that portion. Examples of reasonable cause and good faith: reasonable reliance on the advice of a qualified tax professional who had all relevant facts; a taxpayer's reasonable, good-faith interpretation of an ambiguous rule. The practitioner's advice must be independent (not generated by the taxpayer) and based on full disclosure of facts to qualify as a defense.
explanations.c: While negligence triggers §6662, the reasonable cause exception under §6664(c) IS available to avoid the penalty even for negligent positions, provided the taxpayer demonstrates good faith and reasonable cause. The penalty is not absolute.
explanations.d: The 40% penalty applies specifically to GROSS valuation misstatements (overvaluation or undervaluation by 200%+) — not to general substantial understatements due to negligence. The standard §6662 rate for negligence and/or substantial understatement is 20%.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: IRC §6662/§6663 accuracy-related penalties and authoritative hierarchy — negligence, substantial understatement, fraud penalty; substantial authority, MLTN standards; hierarchy of authority
questions.text: A taxpayer reports no income on their federal tax return, but the IRS determines through examination that the taxpayer willfully failed to report $500,000 of income in a deliberate scheme to defraud the United States. The correct tax liability on the $500,000 is $150,000. Calculate the §6663 civil fraud penalty.

answers.text: $30,000 (20% × $150,000) — the standard accuracy-related penalty rate applies to all underpayments
$150,000 (100% × $150,000) — fraud requires full repayment of the tax as a penalty
$112,500 (75% × $150,000) — the civil fraud penalty under §6663 is 75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud
$500,000 — the civil fraud penalty equals the unreported income, not the tax on it

explanations.a: The 20% rate is the accuracy-related penalty under §6662. The civil fraud penalty under §6663 is 75% — a significantly higher rate designed to deter intentional tax fraud. The §6662 and §6663 penalties do not stack — when fraud is established, §6663 applies instead of §6662.
explanations.b: 100% of the tax is not a recognized civil penalty rate. The maximum civil fraud penalty is 75% under §6663, plus interest on the underpayment.
explanations.c: Section §6663 civil fraud penalty: 75% × underpayment attributable to fraud = 75% × $150,000 = $112,500. Key aspects of §6663: (1) Rate: 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud; (2) Burden of proof: the IRS bears the burden of proving fraud by clear and convincing evidence; (3) Effect: if fraud is established for any portion, the entire underpayment is treated as fraudulent (unless the taxpayer can establish that part of the underpayment is not due to fraud); (4) No reasonable cause defense: unlike §6662, there is no reasonable cause exception to §6663; (5) Criminal vs. civil: §6663 is a CIVIL penalty; criminal tax fraud under §7201 is separate and can result in imprisonment and additional fines; (6) Statute of limitations: no statute of limitations applies to fraudulent returns — the IRS can assess deficiencies at any time.
explanations.d: The civil fraud penalty is calculated on the TAX underpayment (75% × $150,000), not on the unreported income ($500,000). Tax amounts and income amounts are separate figures — the penalty is measured on the tax underpayment.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: IRC §6662/§6663 accuracy-related penalties and authoritative hierarchy — negligence, substantial understatement, fraud penalty; substantial authority, MLTN standards; hierarchy of authority
questions.text: A CPA is advising a client on a tax shelter transaction. The CPA evaluates the position and believes it has a 45% probability of being sustained if challenged. The transaction is a listed transaction designated by the IRS as a tax avoidance scheme. Identify the applicable disclosure standard and assess the risk to both the taxpayer and the CPA.

answers.text: A 45% probability satisfies the substantial authority standard; disclosure is voluntary for tax shelter transactions; the CPA has no additional obligations

Disclosure is only required for listed transactions when the tax benefit exceeds $1,000,000 for individuals; at 45%, the substantial authority standard is met and the taxpayer is fully protected from penalties
The transaction does not require disclosure because the CPA has concluded it has a 45% chance of success, which meets the reasonable basis standard applicable to listed transactions

For listed transactions, both the taxpayer (Form 8886) and the material advisor (Form 8918) must disclose the transaction regardless of probability of success; substantial authority is not sufficient — the more-likely-than-not (MLTN, >50%) standard applies to tax shelter items; at 45%, the MLTN standard is not met, and penalties apply unless the taxpayer has reasonable cause

explanations.a: For TAX SHELTER transactions (including listed transactions), the standard is MORE-LIKELY-THAN-NOT (>50%), not substantial authority (~40%). Additionally, disclosure is MANDATORY, not voluntary, for listed transactions.
explanations.b: There is no $1,000,000 threshold for listed transaction disclosure obligations. ALL participants in listed transactions must disclose regardless of the dollar amount of tax benefit. A 45% probability does not meet the MLTN (>50%) standard required for tax shelter items.
explanations.c: For listed transactions, the disclosure requirement is mandatory under §6011 — it is not avoided by concluding any particular probability of success. The 'reasonable basis' standard (~10%) is the minimum threshold to avoid certain penalties, but it does not eliminate the disclosure obligation for listed transactions.
explanations.d: Analysis of listed transaction obligations: (1) Listed transactions: the IRS formally designates certain transactions as tax avoidance schemes requiring mandatory disclosure. These receive the highest scrutiny level; (2) Taxpayer disclosure: §6011 requires taxpayers participating in listed transactions to attach Form 8886 (Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement) to their return — mandatory regardless of probability; failure to disclose: penalty equal to 75% of the tax benefit ($10,000 minimum for individuals, $25,000 for others); (3) Material advisor disclosure: §6111 requires material advisors (CPAs, attorneys, financial advisors who provide substantial assistance) to file Form 8918 (Material Advisor Disclosure Statement) and maintain lists of clients under §6112; material advisor penalty for non-disclosure: the GREATER of $200,000 or 50% of the fees from the transaction; (4) Penalty standard: for undisclosed tax shelter positions, the penalty standard is MLTN (>50%). At 45%, the MLTN standard is NOT met — §6662A imposes a 20% penalty (or 30% for undisclosed transactions); (5) Both the taxpayer and the CPA face significant penalties even if the transaction has some merit.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Licensing, disciplinary systems and legal duties — state boards of accountancy, CPA licensure, common law duties to clients and third parties, privileged communications §7525, confidentiality
questions.text: Under IRC §7525, what is the scope of the confidentiality privilege for federally authorized tax practitioners (such as enrolled agents and CPAs)?

answers.text: The §7525 privilege covers confidential communications between a federally authorized tax practitioner and a client with respect to tax advice, but it does NOT extend to criminal tax matters, does NOT apply in state court proceedings, and may be waived by the client
The §7525 privilege is identical to the attorney-client privilege — it covers all communications between a tax practitioner and their client, including criminal matters and state court proceedings
The §7525 privilege applies only to written communications — oral tax advice between a practitioner and client is not privileged
The §7525 privilege applies only to enrolled agents — CPAs must rely on state confidentiality laws and cannot claim the federal privilege

explanations.a: IRC §7525 (enacted 1998) extended a limited form of privilege to federally authorized tax practitioners (enrolled agents, CPAs, and others authorized to practice before the IRS). Key characteristics: (1) Scope: applies to confidential communications between a federally authorized tax practitioner and a client concerning tax advice; (2) Limitations: does NOT apply to any criminal matter; does NOT apply in state court proceedings (only in federal proceedings before the IRS and federal courts); CANNOT be used to conceal documents that would otherwise be discoverable; (3) Waiver: the privilege belongs to the client and can be waived by the client; (4) Comparison to attorney-client: the attorney-client privilege is broader — it extends to criminal matters, all courts, and has deeper historical and legal roots; (5) Work-product doctrine: both attorneys and other practitioners may also claim work-product protection for materials prepared in anticipation of litigation.
explanations.b: The §7525 privilege is deliberately narrower than the attorney-client privilege. Unlike attorney-client privilege, §7525 does NOT cover criminal tax matters and does NOT apply in state court proceedings. The attorney-client privilege is broader in scope.
explanations.c: The §7525 privilege is not limited to written communications. Both written and oral confidential communications between the practitioner and client concerning tax advice are potentially privileged. The key requirement is that the communication must be made in confidence for the purpose of seeking or providing tax advice.
explanations.d: Section §7525 applies to ALL federally authorized tax practitioners, including both CPAs and enrolled agents. The IRS designates who qualifies as a 'federally authorized tax practitioner' — it is not limited to enrolled agents.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Licensing, disciplinary systems and legal duties — state boards of accountancy, CPA licensure, common law duties to clients and third parties, privileged communications §7525, confidentiality
questions.text: A CPA prepares financial statements for ABC Corporation, which uses them to obtain a bank loan. The bank later suffers a loss because the financial statements contained material misstatements that the CPA negligently failed to detect. Under the majority rule (Restatement Second of Torts approach), can the bank sue the CPA for negligence?

answers.text: No — under the privity rule (Ultramares doctrine), the CPA is only liable to ABC Corporation since the bank was not in contractual privity with the CPA

Yes — under the majority rule, the CPA is liable to third parties who are members of a specifically foreseen and limited class of persons whom the auditor knew would rely on the financial statements for a specific transaction
No — CPAs are immune from third-party lawsuits unless the third party is specifically named in the engagement letter
Yes — under the most liberal (minority) foreseeability rule, the CPA is liable to any foreseeable user of the financial statements without limitation

explanations.a: The strict privity rule (Ultramares Corp. v. Touche, 1931) holds that a CPA is only liable for negligence to parties in direct privity of contract. Most US states no longer follow the strict Ultramares rule — the majority have adopted a broader standard. Under Ultramares, the bank would have no claim; under the majority rule, the analysis is different.
explanations.b: The majority rule follows the Restatement (Second) of Torts §552 approach: a CPA is liable for negligent misrepresentation to third parties who are members of a LIMITED AND FORESEEABLE CLASS — specifically, persons for whose benefit and guidance the information was supplied, and who the CPA knew (or reasonably should have known) would rely on it for a specific transaction. Analysis: If the CPA knew that ABC Corporation intended to use the financial statements to obtain a bank loan (specific use for a specific class of lenders), the bank falls within the foreseeable class and the CPA may be liable even without privity. If the financial statements were for general use and the CPA had no knowledge of the bank's specific reliance, liability may be limited. This contrasts with: (a) Ultramares (strict privity — most restrictive); (b) Foreseeability rule/Rosenblum v. Adler (most liberal — any reasonably foreseeable user).
explanations.c: There is no general common law immunity for CPAs from third-party lawsuits. Engagement letters define the scope of work and may limit liability, but they do not automatically immunize the CPA from third-party claims. Third-party liability is governed by the applicable standard in the relevant jurisdiction.
explanations.d: The most liberal foreseeability rule (followed by a minority of states including New Jersey under Rosenblum v. Adler) would hold the CPA liable to any reasonably foreseeable user — this is the broadest standard, not the majority rule.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Licensing, disciplinary systems and legal duties — state boards of accountancy, CPA licensure, common law duties to clients and third parties, privileged communications §7525, confidentiality
questions.text: A CPA discovers, while preparing a client's current-year tax return, that the client's prior-year return contained a material error that resulted in a significant tax underpayment. The client refuses to allow the CPA to amend the prior return. What are the CPA's professional responsibilities under Circular 230 and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services (SSTS)?

answers.text: The CPA must immediately notify the IRS of the error — failure to report known client errors is a violation of Circular 230 and could result in the CPA's disbarment
The CPA must withdraw from the engagement immediately — continuing to work with a client who has an unamended error creates strict liability for the CPA

The CPA should promptly advise the client of the error and its consequences, but cannot compel the client to file an amended return; if the client continues to refuse and the error affects the current-year return, the CPA should consider whether to continue the engagement, but the CPA must not notify the IRS without client consent (absent a legal requirement)
The CPA has no obligation regarding prior-year errors discovered while preparing current-year returns — responsibility for prior returns ends when those returns are filed

explanations.a: Circular 230 and the AICPA SSTS do NOT generally require a CPA to notify the IRS of a client's error without the client's consent. The CPA-client relationship includes confidentiality obligations. The CPA's duty is to advise the client, not to report the client to the IRS unilaterally.
explanations.b: Immediate withdrawal is not always required when a client has a prior-year error. Withdrawal may be appropriate if the client insists on perpetuating the error in the current return, but the FIRST required step is to advise the client and seek their correction. Mandatory immediate withdrawal is an overstatement of the CPA's obligations.
explanations.c: CPA responsibilities when prior-year errors are discovered: Under Circular 230 §10.21 and AICPA SSTS No. 6: (1) Notification: the CPA must promptly advise the client of the error and its potential consequences (additional tax, interest, and penalties if discovered by the IRS); (2) No compulsion: the CPA cannot force the client to file an amended return — the client has the legal right to make that decision; (3) Confidentiality: the CPA generally cannot notify the IRS of the error without the client's consent (§7525 privilege; professional confidentiality rules); exceptions exist for suspected money laundering, terrorist financing, or other illegal activities where mandatory reporting may be required; (4) Current-year consideration: if the prior-year error affects items on the current-year return (e.g., carryforward amounts), the CPA must address the impact on the current return accurately; (5) Withdrawal: if the client insists on carrying incorrect amounts from the prior return into the current return (perpetuating the error), the CPA may need to withdraw from the engagement to avoid association with an inaccurate return.
explanations.d: While the CPA's legal liability for a prior-year return diminishes over time, the professional responsibility to advise clients of discovered errors applies regardless of when the error occurred. Discovering and remaining silent about a material error violates professional standards.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Licensing, disciplinary systems and legal duties — state boards of accountancy, CPA licensure, common law duties to clients and third parties, privileged communications §7525, confidentiality
questions.text: A CPA is auditing Retail Co., a public company. During the audit, the CPA discovers evidence that management has been embezzling funds through a complex scheme involving false vendor invoices. The scheme has been concealed through fraudulent journal entries. Management refuses to disclose the fraud and threatens legal action against the CPA firm if it reports to authorities. Identify the CPA's legal obligations and the potential consequences of various courses of action.

answers.text: The CPA must maintain absolute confidentiality — all information learned during an audit is protected and may never be disclosed to any party outside the engagement
The CPA's only obligation is to disclose the fraud to the engagement partner and firm management — external reporting is prohibited by attorney-client privilege analogies
The CPA should issue an unqualified (clean) audit opinion to preserve the audit relationship and then privately warn investors through informal channels

For a public company, the CPA's obligations are governed by SOX §10A: the CPA must report the illegal act to the audit committee if management fails to take corrective action; if the audit committee fails to act, the CPA must consider resigning and notifying the SEC; failure to comply with §10A can result in loss of PCAOB registration and civil liability

explanations.a: Confidentiality obligations are not absolute for public company auditors. SOX §10A creates specific mandatory reporting obligations that override general confidentiality when illegal acts are discovered in a public company audit.
explanations.b: §7525 privilege does not apply to public company audits in the manner suggested. More importantly, the SOX §10A reporting obligations are statutory requirements that supersede normal confidentiality rules for the specific context of public company audits where illegal acts are discovered.
explanations.c: Issuing an unqualified opinion on financial statements containing material fraud concealed by management would be fraudulent. The CPA would be complicit in the fraud and face personal liability under securities laws, Rule 10b-5, and professional standards.
explanations.d: SOX §10A (Sarbanes-Oxley Act, 2002) requirements for auditors of public companies when illegal acts are discovered: (1) Initial discovery: the auditor must determine whether the illegal act has occurred; (2) Reporting to management/audit committee: the auditor must report the matter to senior management and, if not corrected, to the audit committee within one business day; (3) Audit committee inaction: if the audit committee fails to take timely remedial action, the auditor must either: (a) resign from the engagement, or (b) provide written notice to the SEC within one business day; (4) SEC notification: if the auditor resigns and the SEC is not promptly notified, the SEC has authority to require the company to notify the SEC; (5) Consequences for non-compliance: loss of PCAOB registration (required for public company audit), SEC enforcement action, civil liability under securities laws; (6) Management threats: management's threats of legal action do not relieve the auditor of §10A obligations — such threats may themselves be evidence of the illegal nature of the conduct. The CPA cannot ignore the fraud or issue a clean opinion with knowledge of undisclosed material fraud.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Federal tax procedures — IRS audit types, 30-day letter, 90-day letter, appeals, Tax Court vs. District Court vs. Court of Federal Claims; §6501 statute of limitations; FBAR
questions.text: Under IRC §6501, what is the general statute of limitations for the IRS to assess a federal income tax deficiency?

answers.text: Three years from the later of the date the return was filed or the original due date of the return
One year from the date the return was filed or its due date, whichever is later
There is no statute of limitations — the IRS can assess a deficiency at any time regardless of when the return was filed
Six years from the date the return was filed, regardless of whether any income was omitted

explanations.a: Under §6501(a), the general statute of limitations for IRS assessment of a tax deficiency is THREE YEARS from the later of: (a) the date the return was actually filed, or (b) the return's original due date (not counting extensions). Example: a calendar-year 2023 return due April 15, 2024, filed on March 1, 2024 — the 3-year period runs from April 15, 2024 (the due date), expiring April 15, 2027. Extended limitations: §6501(e)(1): 6 years when the taxpayer omits from gross income an amount exceeding 25% of the gross income stated on the return; §6501(c)(1): NO statute of limitations for fraudulent returns filed with intent to evade tax; §6501(c)(3): NO statute of limitations when no return has been filed. Note: if the taxpayer and IRS agree to extend the period, they can execute a Form 872 (Consent to Extend the Time to Assess Tax).
explanations.b: One year is significantly shorter than the actual statute of limitations. The IRS needs sufficient time to audit returns after they are filed — a one-year window would be inadequate for the complexity of many tax returns.
explanations.c: This describes the treatment for fraudulent returns or failure to file. The general rule for properly filed returns is a 3-year limitations period — the IRS cannot assess indefinitely for good-faith filers.
explanations.d: Six years is the EXTENDED statute of limitations that applies when gross income is substantially omitted (>25% omitted). It is not the general rule.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Federal tax procedures — IRS audit types, 30-day letter, 90-day letter, appeals, Tax Court vs. District Court vs. Court of Federal Claims; §6501 statute of limitations; FBAR
questions.text: A taxpayer receives a 90-day letter (Statutory Notice of Deficiency) from the IRS proposing a $25,000 deficiency. The taxpayer disagrees with the IRS's position. In which forum can the taxpayer contest the deficiency WITHOUT first paying the disputed tax?

answers.text: US District Court — taxpayers can challenge IRS deficiencies without payment and have the right to a jury trial
US Tax Court — taxpayers may petition the Tax Court within 90 days of the notice of deficiency and contest the tax without paying it first
US Court of Federal Claims — this court specializes in tax refund cases and does not require prepayment
All three courts — any federal court allows taxpayers to contest tax deficiencies before payment under the Anti-Injunction Act

explanations.a: US District Court requires the taxpayer to PAY the tax in full, then file a claim for refund with the IRS, wait for the IRS to deny it (or wait 6 months), and then sue for a refund. Prepayment is required for District Court. The jury trial right is available, but only after payment.
explanations.b: The US Tax Court is the ONLY federal court where a taxpayer can contest a tax deficiency WITHOUT first paying the disputed amount. Process: (1) IRS issues 90-day letter (Statutory Notice of Deficiency); (2) Taxpayer has 90 days (150 days if addressed to a person outside the US) to file a petition with Tax Court; (3) Tax Court adjudicates the dispute before any tax must be paid (prepayment is NOT required); (4) Tax Court is a specialized court with expertise in tax law; (5) No jury trial available in Tax Court (judge decides); (6) The Small Tax Case Division (S cases) is available for deficiencies of $50,000 or less — less formal, faster, but decisions are not appealable. If the taxpayer does not petition Tax Court within the 90-day window, the IRS assesses the deficiency and collection proceedings can begin.
explanations.c: US Court of Federal Claims also requires PREPAYMENT of the disputed tax before the court has jurisdiction. Like District Court, it is a refund forum — the taxpayer pays first, then sues for a refund.
explanations.d: The Anti-Injunction Act (§7421) generally PROHIBITS courts from enjoining tax collection — it does not allow all courts to hear pre-payment challenges. Only the Tax Court provides a pre-payment forum through the deficiency petition process.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Federal tax procedures — IRS audit types, 30-day letter, 90-day letter, appeals, Tax Court vs. District Court vs. Court of Federal Claims; §6501 statute of limitations; FBAR
questions.text: A US citizen has the following foreign bank accounts during the calendar year: Account A in Switzerland with a peak balance of $7,000; Account B in Germany with a peak balance of $5,000; Account C in Canada with a peak balance of $3,000. Determine the FBAR filing requirement.

answers.text: No FBAR filing required — each individual account is below the $10,000 threshold and is therefore exempt
FBAR filing is required only for Account A (Switzerland) because it has the highest balance; the other accounts are below individual account thresholds
FBAR filing is required because the aggregate maximum balances of all three accounts ($15,000) exceed $10,000 during the calendar year — all accounts must be reported on a single FBAR
FBAR filing is only required for accounts in countries without US tax treaties — Switzerland, Germany, and Canada all have treaties, so no FBAR is required

explanations.a: The $10,000 FBAR threshold is based on the AGGREGATE maximum balance of ALL foreign financial accounts during the calendar year — not on any individual account balance. Even if no single account exceeds $10,000, FBAR may be required if the total aggregate exceeds the threshold.
explanations.b: There is no concept of 'highest balance account only' in FBAR rules. The FBAR requires reporting of ALL foreign financial accounts when the aggregate threshold is met — all accounts must be included on the single FBAR filing (FinCEN Form 114).
explanations.c: FBAR (Foreign Bank Account Report) requirements under 31 USC §5314 and FinCEN regulations: (1) Who must file: US persons (citizens, resident aliens, domestic entities) who have a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts; (2) Threshold: if the aggregate maximum value of ALL foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at ANY point during the calendar year; (3) This taxpayer: $7,000 + $5,000 + $3,000 = $15,000 aggregate maximum — exceeds $10,000; (4) Filing requirement: FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR) must be filed electronically with FinCEN; (5) Due date: April 15 (same as individual income tax return), with automatic extension to October 15; (6) ALL three accounts (A, B, and C) must be reported on the single FBAR — not just the Swiss account; (7) Penalties: civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation for non-willful; criminal penalties for willful violations.
explanations.d: Tax treaty status has no bearing on FBAR filing requirements. FBAR is a Bank Secrecy Act reporting requirement, not an income tax filing. Countries with or without US tax treaties are subject to the same FBAR aggregate threshold rules.

questions.name: Ethics, Professional Responsibilities and Federal Tax Procedures
questions.keyword: Federal tax procedures — IRS audit types, 30-day letter, 90-day letter, appeals, Tax Court vs. District Court vs. Court of Federal Claims; §6501 statute of limitations; FBAR
questions.text: An IRS field examination concludes with a 30-day letter proposing a $40,000 deficiency. The taxpayer disputes the IRS's position. Trace the available administrative and judicial remedies in sequence, and identify the key strategic difference between the Tax Court and District Court options.

answers.text: The 30-day letter is the final IRS determination; the taxpayer must immediately pay the $40,000 or petition the Tax Court
All disputes must be resolved through IRS Appeals before any judicial proceeding is allowed; Tax Court petitions are only available after mandatory Appeals review
The only option after a 30-day letter is to petition the Tax Court immediately — IRS Appeals does not handle field examination cases

The taxpayer may: (1) File a written protest and appeal to the IRS Office of Appeals within 30 days; (2) If Appeals does not resolve it, the IRS issues a 90-day letter; (3) The taxpayer may then petition the Tax Court (no prepayment) within 90 days; or (4) Pay the tax, file a claim for refund, and if denied, sue in District Court (jury trial available) or Court of Federal Claims; strategic choice: Tax Court = no prepayment but no jury; District Court = prepayment required but jury trial possible

explanations.a: The 30-day letter is NOT the final IRS determination — it is a preliminary notice that invites the taxpayer to either agree to the proposed changes or appeal administratively. The IRS Office of Appeals is available after a 30-day letter, and the 90-day letter (Statutory Notice of Deficiency) is a subsequent step.
explanations.b: Appeals is not mandatory — taxpayers can bypass Appeals and go directly to Tax Court by not responding to the 30-day letter and waiting for the 90-day letter. However, bypassing Appeals is generally not strategically advisable because Appeals often settles cases on better terms than litigation.
explanations.c: IRS Office of Appeals DOES handle field examination cases. After receiving a 30-day letter, taxpayers routinely file protests to Appeals — this is a common and effective step. Bypassing Appeals and going directly to Tax Court is permitted but waives the opportunity for administrative settlement.
explanations.d: Complete sequence of remedies: (1) 30-day letter received: the IRS proposes a $40,000 deficiency and invites the taxpayer to agree, meet with the examining agent, or appeal within 30 days; (2) IRS Office of Appeals: taxpayer files a written protest (required for amounts >$25,000) within 30 days — Appeals officers are independent of Examination and have authority to settle cases based on hazards of litigation; (3) 90-day letter (Notice of Deficiency): if no agreement is reached at Appeals (or if the taxpayer bypasses Appeals), the IRS issues the 90-day letter, triggering the taxpayer's right to petition Tax Court; (4) Tax Court petition: must be filed within 90 days of the 90-day letter — NO prepayment required; no jury trial; specialized tax judges; decisions are appealable to the Circuit Courts of Appeal; (5) District Court or Court of Federal Claims: taxpayer pays the $40,000, files a claim for refund with the IRS, waits for rejection (or 6 months), then sues — District Court: jury trial available; Court of Federal Claims: no jury. Strategic considerations: (a) If the law is favorable but the facts are disputed → District Court (jury may decide facts more favorably than a judge); (b) If prepayment is a financial hardship → Tax Court; (c) If the Circuit precedent is favorable → choose the court in the applicable circuit.
